item.title: The Last Ice on Puncak Jaya
item.summary: Ice near the summit of the Indonesian mountain peak has shrunk to scattered patches too small to flow like glaciers.
item.page_text:
Ice near the summit of the Indonesian mountain peak has shrunk to scattered patches too small to flow like glaciers.
On the island of New Guinea, Indonesia’s Sudirman Range is one of the few places near the equator that have long held ice year-round. But near the summit of Puncak Jaya, the ice has dwindled to patches too small to flow like glaciers.
Positioned in the tropics beside the largest expanse of warm ocean water on Earth, the range’s glaciers lie near the warmest conditions in which ice can survive year-round. Scientists have described these glaciers as high-altitude “ canaries in the coal mine ,” alongside other tropical ice such as the remnants of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, and the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania.
The change on Puncak Jaya is visible in this image pair, acquired in 1988 by the TM (Thematic Mapper) on Landsat 5 (left) and in 2026 by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 (right). The false-color images help distinguish areas of ice (light blue) from exposed bedrock (brown). Clouds appear white and vegetation green.
In 1988, the glaciers covered about 4.31 square kilometers (1.66 square miles), according to Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist at the Indonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics (BMKG). By September 2025, satellite and aerial data showed that only about 0.09 square kilometers (0.03 square miles) remained—an area equivalent to about a dozen soccer fields. That’s roughly 2 percent of the 1988 extent. An aerial survey planned for December should yield an estimate of how much ice remains in 2026, Permana said.
The glaciers have thinned, too. Measurements at the primary monitoring site on the East Northwall Firn showed a drop from 32 meters (105 feet) thick in 2010 to 4 meters (13 feet) in 2023, Permana said. By November 2024, the ice at this site was gone.
As the glaciers thin, they also break apart, and each new fragment adds exposed edges where ice can melt, compounding the losses. In the 2026 Landsat image, freshly uncovered bedrock appears between the remnants. Snow still falls in the area, but it doesn’t last long enough on the bare rock to build up into new ice.
“It’s a house of cards problem,” said Chris Shuman, a retired University of Maryland glaciologist who has tracked Puncak Jaya’s glaciers in satellite imagery. “Once this process gets going, there’s really no turning back.”
To qualify as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight, and it needs an area where snow builds up faster than it melts. Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows.
“While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana said.
As for the remaining patches of ice, time will tell how long they last. Recent satellite studies suggest complete disappearance of the main glacial ice areas could occur around 2030. Permana noted that BMKG estimates suggest they could be gone much sooner, hastened by the current El Niño .
Past El Niño years have hit these glaciers especially hard. As the air warms, the freezing level rises above the summit, so precipitation falls as rain instead of snow. That means less fresh white snow that normally reflects sunlight and shields the ice, leaving darker surfaces that absorb more heat and melt faster. During the 2015-2016 El Niño, the ice thinned about five times faster than usual , losing roughly 5.3 meters (17 feet) of thickness in a single year. The 2023-2024 El Niño brought another bout of rapid thinning, about 2 to 4 meters (7 to 13 feet) per year.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . Story by Kathryn Hansen.

item.title: Satellite images showing the aftermath of the attack on the Russian port of Ust-Luga have ...
item.summary: This was reported by "Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty," UNN writes. Details. The released satellite images show 5 storage tanks for petroleum products ...
item.page_text:
Following the Ukrainian attack on the port of Ust-Luga, at least five tanks containing petroleum products were completely
destroyed by fire. Russia reported three people injured.
As a result of a Ukrainian attack on the Russian port of Ust-Luga in the Leningrad region on November 11, at least 5 tanks containing petroleum products burned out completely. The extent of the damage became known after new satellite images emerged. This was reported by "Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty," UNN writes.
The released satellite images show 5 storage tanks for petroleum products completely destroyed by fire. Traces of foam used by firefighters to extinguish the blaze are visible near several other tanks.
The images made it possible to assess the consequences of the strike, as Russian authorities had previously reported only a fire in the port area.
During the night of November 11, a massive fire broke out in the port following the attack. The first footage of the fire appeared during the night, and at around 6:00 a.m., the governor of the Leningrad region confirmed the fire.
Later, Russian authorities reported 3 people injured. NASA satellites also recorded a large fire at the port.
The fire was so large that its glow could reportedly be seen even by residents of neighboring Estonia.
"The Night the Baltic Caught Fire": General Staff Shows Strike on Ust-Luga Port in Russia 12.11.26, 04:53 • 24805 views

item.title: Yosemite Valley LiDAR Map - Stephen Conklin
item.summary: Yosemite Valley LiDAR Map . A 243-million-point airborne LiDAR survey turned into a detail map, a 3D view, and a layer-by-layer processing stack ...
item.page_text:
An airborne LiDAR survey of Yosemite Valley, flown by the National Center for Airborne Laser Mapping (NCALM), holds about 243 million laser returns, classified into two classes: ground and unclassified. This map turns those points into three views on one sheet: a 3D view up the valley, a detail map of the valley floor, and an exploded stack that shows how each layer was made.
All layers are in UTM Zone 11N (EPSG:26911).
The eight steps above, stacked from the point cloud at the bottom to the finished map at the top, for an area around Yosemite Village. Rendered in Blender from layers exported out of QGIS.
The 2D maps from the same layout: a detail map of the valley floor and an overview of the full survey.
LiDAR processing, terrain analysis, and cartography
LiDAR: National Center for Airborne Laser Mapping (NCALM), distributed by OpenTopography (doi:10.5069/G9GQ6VP3). NCALM funding from NSF's Division of Earth Sciences, Instrumentation and Facilities Program (EAR-1043051); OpenTopography services supported by NSF awards 2410799, 2410800, and 2410801. Roads, trails, and buildings © OpenStreetMap contributors. California outline: U.S. Census.
A low 3D view across the valley floor. Every tree is drawn from the LiDAR points themselves rather than from a symbol.

item.title: An Inverted Earth You Can Explore
item.summary: In honor of the #30DayMapChallenge's Inverted theme, Tripgeo has released Atlantis - the Inverted Earth . I've seen a few maps that swap the Earth's land and oceans around, turning familiar continents into vast underwater worlds and ocean basins into towering mountain ranges. But this is the first I've encountered that lets you actually explore the resulting world from the cockpit of your own submarine. In Atlantis: The World Turned Over , the oceans have drained onto the continents, leaving the former seabed exposed as enormous mountain ranges. Meanwhile, every city on Earth has been submerged beneath the newly formed oceans. Your vehicle for exploring this topsy-turvy planet is the Nereid, a fully navigable submarine that you can pilot directly in your browser. You can dive through the drowned streets of familiar cities, explore submerged urban landscapes and venture into the newly flooded continental interiors. You can even use sonar to sound the depths of the inverted world's ocean trenches. One of the most intriguing aspects is seeing familiar places transformed by this geographical reversal. item.page_text:
November 15, 2026 at 11:16 PM • 13165 переглядiв
As a result of a Ukrainian attack on the Russian port of Ust-Luga in the Leningrad region on November 11, at least 5 tanks containing petroleum products burned out completely. The extent of the damage became known after new satellite images emerged. This was reported by "Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty," UNN writes.
The released satellite images show 5 storage tanks for petroleum products completely destroyed by fire. Traces of foam used by firefighters to extinguish the blaze are visible near several other tanks.
The images made it possible to assess the consequences of the strike, as Russian authorities had previously reported only a fire in the port area.
During the night of November 11, a massive fire broke out in the port following the attack. The first footage of the fire appeared during the night, and at around 6:00 a.m., the governor of the Leningrad region confirmed the fire.
Later, Russian authorities reported 3 people injured. NASA satellites also recorded a large fire at the port.
The fire was so large that its glow could reportedly be seen even by residents of neighboring Estonia.
